newsitem.title: USA: MCI jumps into Internet policy disputes.
newsitem.headline: MCI jumps into Internet policy disputes.

text.p: MCI Communications Corp on Monday released a wide-ranging Internet policy statement that thrust the company into the middle of half a dozen raging debates over appropriate regulation of cyberspace.

The telecommunications giant, which runs one of the largest parts of the Internet's backbone connection, supported voluntary, self-regulation in most cases and said government rules would only stifle the vast computer network's growth.
"The Internet moves faster than government," Jonathan Sallet, MCI's chief policy counsel, told reporters at a news briefing here.
"An attempt to have governmental regulation lead today will only slow down and obstruct innovation on the Internet," he said.
Although generally consistent with the Clinton administration's Internet policy announced on July 1, the MCI approach immediately drew fire on several fronts.

MCI supported industry efforts to protect the privacy rights of Internet users through technology and disclosure. The company rejected as unworkable the European Union's Privacy Directive limiting and regulating the sale of personal information about consumers.

"Current U.S. law protecting individual privacy is basically sound," said Vinton Cerf, MCI senior vice president and one of the inventors of the software underlying the Internet. "In other parts of the world, privacy concerns have led to legislated and potentially bureaucratic methods that do not comport well with the fast moving and highly connected Internet environment."
Clinton's policy paper generally backed the laissez-faire approach, with a possible exception made for protecting the privacy of children, but some privacy advocates want new laws enacted.
"What's clear at this point is that the law has failed to keep up with the technology," said Marc Rotenberg, director of the non-profit Electronic Privacy Information Center in Washington, D.C.
"Even as companies are developing new policies, I don't think these policies will be an adequate substitute for consumers who need legal protection for their personal information," he said.

MCI broke with the Clinton approach on computer encoding technology. The administration forbids the export of most strong encryption, programs which scramble information and render it unreadable without a password or software "key."

MCI's Cerf said strong encryption was essential to the development of electronic commerce. "Commerce on the Internet cannot flourish globally without widespread availability of high-grade cryptographic hardware and software," he said.

Strong encryption can be exported if the product allows the government to crack the codes by gaining access to the keys. Cerf said there was no market demand for mandatory key recovery products that allowed government access.

Administration officials countered that key recovery, needed to allow law enforcement agencies to decode communications among criminals, could be incorporated into the infrastructure that is being built to accomodate electronic commerce.

"All we're trying to do is to piggyback on the systems that have to be developed in order to meet law enforcement needs," Under Secretary of Commerce William Reinsch told Reuters. "I don't think that is incompatible with what they want to accomplish."
MCI also struck out against taxation of Internet commerce, a position opposed by some state and local government groups.

On the issue of intellectual property, MCI asked Congress to clarify treaties adopted by the World Intellectual Property Organization in order to free Internet service providers from strict liability for copyright violations that occur over the Internet. Major entertainment producers and software companies have asked Congress to tighten the treaties.
And MCI continued to back a controversial plan to expand the Internet address system that is opposed by some Internet service providers.
On a less controversial topic, MCI also said it would refuse to host Internet sites that allow gambling or other wagering activities.
--Aaron Pressman((202-898-8312))
